name: slots.courseSpecifics
description: The pupils are in Years 7–9 (ages 11–14) of secondary school in England and follow the national curriculum for mathematics at key stage 3. There is no national exam at the end of key stage 3: schools assess pupils themselves, and the course leads on to GCSE mathematics in Years 10 and 11. The curriculum says calculators must not replace written and mental methods, so unless a node says otherwise, expect the pupil to work by hand and show the working, and keep the calculator for checking and for π, roots and trigonometry. Use the conventions of English schools: a decimal point (3.5), commas in large numbers (12,500), coordinates as (2, 3), y = mx + c, the nth term, BIDMAS, metric units, and money in pounds and pence (£4.50).

description: KS3; Year 7; Year 8; Year 9; secondary maths; national curriculum; England; place value; prime factorisation; HCF and LCM; standard form; fractions; percentages; ratio; proportion; algebra; linear equations; nth term; straight-line graphs; y = mx + c; quadratic graphs; angles; constructions; area; volume; Pythagoras' theorem; trigonometry; probability; Venn diagrams; averages; scatter graphs

name: Place value
description:
Place value: the value a digit has because of its position; each place is worth ten times the place to its right, so in 3,407.25 the 4 is worth 400 and the 5 is worth 5 hundredths.
Decimal places: the places to the right of the decimal point, worth tenths, hundredths, thousandths and so on.

name: Negative numbers and the number line
description:
Negative number: a number less than zero, such as −4, written with a minus sign.
Number line: a line on which every number has its place, getting larger to the right; of two numbers, the one further to the right is larger, so −2 > −7.

name: Symbols for comparing numbers
description:
=: is equal to
≠: is not equal to
<: is less than
>: is greater than
≤: is less than or equal to
≥: is greater than or equal to

name: Multiplication facts up to 12 × 12
description: every product a × b where a and b are whole numbers from 2 to 12, and the division facts that go with them, such as 72 ÷ 8 = 9

name: Fractions, mixed numbers and reciprocals
description:
Fraction: a number written a/b, meaning a parts when one whole is split into b equal parts; it also means a ÷ b.
Equivalent fractions: fractions that name the same number, such as 2/3 and 8/12; multiplying or dividing the numerator and denominator by the same number gives an equivalent fraction.
Improper fraction and mixed number: an improper fraction has a numerator at least as large as its denominator, such as 11/4, and can be written as a mixed number, 2¾.
Reciprocal: the number you multiply by to get 1; the reciprocal of 4 is 1/4, and the reciprocal of 3/5 is 5/3.

name: Order integers, decimals and fractions
description: order a mixed set of positive and negative integers, decimals and fractions, place them on a number line, and compare them using =, ≠, <, >, ≤ and ≥.
instruction: Give the pupil a mixed list such as −0.4, 3/8, −1/2, 0.38, −0.45 and 0.4 to put in order from smallest to largest, and ask them to show how they compared the trickiest pair. Then give a few pairs to compare with the right symbol, including two negatives such as −3.2 and −3.15, and a pair where the fraction is hard to judge, such as 3/7 and 0.45.

name: Factors, multiples and primes
description:
Factor (or divisor): a whole number that divides another exactly; the factors of 12 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12.
Multiple: the result of multiplying a number by a whole number; the multiples of 6 are 6, 12, 18, …
Prime number: a whole number greater than 1 whose only factors are 1 and itself; 1 is not prime.
Highest common factor (HCF): the largest number that is a factor of each of two or more numbers.
Lowest common multiple (LCM): the smallest number that is a multiple of each of two or more numbers.

name: Powers and roots
description:
Power: a number written with an index, aⁿ, meaning n copies of a multiplied together; 2⁵ = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 32, and 5 is the index.
Square root: √a is the non-negative number whose square is a, so √49 = 7.
Cube root and higher roots: ∛a is the number whose cube is a, so ∛64 = 4; in the same way, the fourth root of 81 is 3.

name: Write a number as a product of prime factors
description: write a whole number as a product of its prime factors, using a factor tree or repeated division, give the answer in index form, such as 360 = 2³ × 3² × 5, and explain why every whole number greater than 1 has only one prime factorisation.
instruction: Start with 84 and let the pupil build a factor tree, then ask them to build a different tree for the same number and notice that the primes at the end are the same (2² × 3 × 7). Then give 252 and 1,000 to write in index form. Finish by asking which number has the prime factorisation 2³ × 5 × 7 (it is 280).

name: Find the HCF and LCM
description: find the highest common factor and lowest common multiple of two or three numbers, by listing or from their prime factorisations, and use them to solve problems.
instruction: Give the pupil 36 and 60 and ask for the HCF and the LCM, first by listing and then from the prime factorisations, perhaps sorted in a Venn diagram (HCF 12, LCM 180). Then set a word problem: one bus leaves the station every 12 minutes and another every 18 minutes; if they leave together at 9:00, when do they next leave together? (9:36.) Check that the pupil can tell which of the two a problem is asking for.

name: Calculate with negative numbers
description: add, subtract, multiply and divide positive and negative integers, such as −7 − (−3), −4 × −6 and 18 ÷ −3.
instruction: Give the pupil a short mixed set, such as −7 + 12, −3 − 8, 5 − (−4), −6 × −7 and −42 ÷ 6, and ask for each answer and how they thought about it, using the number line for adding and subtracting. Watch for −3 − 8 being treated as −3 + 8. Then ask them to make up three different calculations with negative numbers whose answer is −12.

name: Use written methods for whole numbers and decimals
description: add, subtract, multiply and divide whole numbers and decimals with formal written methods: column addition and subtraction, long multiplication, and short and long division.
instruction: Give the pupil, without a calculator, 403.6 − 87.95, 347 × 28, 2.6 × 0.35, 1,512 ÷ 24 and 47 ÷ 4. Ask them to set each out in full and to estimate first so they can check the size of the answer (315.65, 9,716, 0.91, 63 and 11.75). In the decimal multiplication, ask how they decided where the decimal point goes.

name: Calculate with fractions
description: add, subtract, multiply and divide fractions, including improper fractions, mixed numbers and negative fractions, and give the answer in its simplest form.
instruction: Give the pupil, without a calculator, 2/3 + 3/4, 3½ − 1⅚, 2⅖ × 5/6 and 3/4 ÷ 9/10, and ask them to show each step and simplify (1 5/12, 1⅔, 2 and 5/6). Then try one with a negative, such as −1/2 − 1/3. Ask them to explain why dividing 3/4 by 9/10 gives an answer bigger than 3/4.

name: Use the priority of operations
description: work out calculations with several operations in the conventional order, brackets first, then powers and roots, then multiplication and division, then addition and subtraction (BIDMAS), including calculations with negative numbers and fraction bars.
instruction: Give the pupil 5 + 4 × 3, (5 + 4) × 3, 20 − 3 × (5 − 2)², 36 ÷ 4 × 3 and √(9 + 16), and ask for each answer and the order they worked in (17, 27, −7, 27 and 5). Ask what (−3)² and −3² are and why they differ (9 and −9). Then give 2 + 3 × 4 − 1 = 19 and ask where to put brackets to make it true.

name: Calculate with powers and roots
description: evaluate powers with positive, zero and negative integer indices, such as 2⁵, 7⁰ and 10⁻³, find square, cube and higher roots, and tell an exact value such as √20 from a decimal approximation such as 4.47.
instruction: Give the pupil 2⁵, 4³, 10⁻², 5⁰ and 2⁻³ to evaluate, and ask them to explain the zero and negative indices from the pattern 2³, 2², 2¹, 2⁰, 2⁻¹, …, where each step divides by 2. Then ask for ∛125, the fourth root of 16, and the two numbers whose square is 49. Finish by asking which is exact, √20 or 4.47, and why the calculator's answer is only an approximation.

name: Standard form
description: Standard form: a number written as A × 10ⁿ, where 1 ≤ A < 10 and n is an integer; 4,700,000 = 4.7 × 10⁶ and 0.00032 = 3.2 × 10⁻⁴.

name: Convert and compare numbers in standard form
description: write large and small numbers in standard form and back again, and order and compare numbers given in standard form.
instruction: Give the pupil numbers to convert each way, such as 63,000, 0.0009, 5.06 × 10⁴ and 7 × 10⁻³. Then give a list to put in order, such as 3.1 × 10⁵, 9.8 × 10⁴, 2.5 × 10⁻² and 4 × 10⁻³, and ask why 9.8 × 10⁴ is smaller than 3.1 × 10⁵ even though 9.8 is bigger than 3.1. Include a number that is not properly in standard form, such as 34 × 10³, and ask them to correct it.

name: Convert between fractions and decimals
description: convert between fractions and terminating decimals, such as 3/8 = 0.375 and 3.5 = 7/2, using place value or division.
instruction: Give the pupil decimals to write as fractions in their simplest form, such as 0.6, 0.45, 0.375 and 2.25, and fractions to write as decimals, such as 7/20, 5/8 and 9/4, without a calculator. Ask them to explain one conversion using place value (0.45 is 45 hundredths) and one using division (5/8 means 5 ÷ 8).

name: Percentage
description: Percentage: a number of parts per hundred, so 35% means 35/100 = 0.35; 100% is the whole amount, and a percentage greater than 100%, such as 150%, means more than the whole.

name: Find a fraction or percentage of an amount
description: find a fraction or a percentage of an amount, using mental methods, written methods or a decimal multiplier, such as 3/5 of £45 or 17.5% of 80 kg.
instruction: Give the pupil amounts to work out without a calculator, such as 3/5 of £45, 15% of 260, 2.5% of 80 kg and 120% of £35, and ask how they built each one up from 10%, 5% and 1%, or from the fraction (£27, 39, 2 kg and £42). Then show that 15% of 260 is the same as 0.15 × 260, and let them use that method on a calculator for 17.5% of £64.80 (£11.34).

name: Round numbers and estimate answers
description: round numbers and measures to a given number of decimal places or significant figures, choose a sensible degree of accuracy for an answer, and estimate the result of a calculation by rounding each number to one significant figure.
instruction: Give the pupil numbers to round, such as 3.4672 to 2 decimal places, 0.003079 to 2 significant figures and 48,615 to 1 significant figure (3.47, 0.0031 and 50,000), and ask them to explain how significant figures are counted when a number starts with zeros. Then ask them to estimate 38.7 × 5.12 ÷ 0.198 by rounding each number to 1 significant figure (40 × 5 ÷ 0.2 = 1,000), and to compare with the calculator answer.

name: Write an error interval
description: write the interval of values that a number rounded to a given accuracy could have come from, using inequality notation such as 6.35 ≤ x < 6.45, and explain why one end is included and the other is not.
instruction: Tell the pupil that a length is 6.4 cm to 1 decimal place and ask for its error interval. Then do the same for a mass of 300 g to the nearest 10 g (295 ≤ m < 305) and a crowd of 50,000 to 1 significant figure (45,000 ≤ n < 55,000). Ask why 6.45 is not included in the interval for 6.4. If that goes well, ask for the greatest possible perimeter of a square whose side is 6.4 cm to 1 decimal place, and why the length can get as close as you like to 25.8 cm without reaching it.

name: Algebraic notation
description:
Product notation: letters written side by side are multiplied, so ab means a × b, and 3y means 3 × y, the same as y + y + y.
Index notation in algebra: a² means a × a, a³ means a × a × a, and a²b means a × a × b.
Division notation: a/b means a ÷ b, and a coefficient is written as a fraction rather than a decimal, as in ½x.

name: Term, expression, equation, formula and inequality
description:
Term: a single number or letter, or numbers and letters multiplied together, such as 5, x or −3ab.
Expression: one or more terms combined with + or −, such as 4x − 7, with no equals sign.
Equation: a statement that two expressions are equal, true only for particular values of the letter, such as 2x + 1 = 9.
Formula: a rule that shows how one quantity is worked out from others, such as A = lw.
Inequality: a statement that one expression is less than or greater than another, such as x + 3 > 7.
Like terms: terms with exactly the same letters raised to the same powers, such as 3x²y and −5x²y.
Factor of an expression: a number, letter or expression that multiplies to make it; in 3(x + 2), the factors are 3 and (x + 2).

name: Substitute into expressions and formulae
description: substitute numbers, including negative numbers and decimals, into expressions and formulae, among them formulae from science such as v = u + at and F = ma, and work out the value.
instruction: Give the pupil a = 3, b = −2 and c = 0.5, and ask for 4a − b, ab², a² + 3c and (a − b)/c, writing the substitution with brackets round the negative number (14, 12, 10.5 and 10). Then give a science formula, v = u + at with u = 4, a = −1.5 and t = 6, and ask for v and what a negative answer means (v = −5).

name: Simplify by collecting like terms
description: simplify an expression by collecting like terms, including terms with powers and products of letters, such as 4x² + 3x − x² − 7x.
instruction: Give the pupil expressions to simplify, such as 5a + 3b − 2a + b, 4x² + 3x − x² − 7x and 2ab + 3ba − ab (3a + 4b, 3x² − 4x and 4ab), and ask them to explain which terms can be collected and why. Include x + x² and ask why it cannot be simplified.

name: Expand a single bracket
description: multiply a single term over a bracket, including negative terms and letters, such as −3(2x − 5) and x(x + 4), and simplify expressions with more than one bracket.
instruction: Give the pupil 4(3x − 2), −2(x − 5), x(x + 7) and 3(2y + 1) − 2(y − 4) to expand and simplify (12x − 8, −2x + 10, x² + 7x and 4y + 11). Ask them to show each product, and check the sign of the last term in −2(x − 5) in particular. Ask them to check one answer by putting the same number into both forms.

name: Factorise by taking out a common factor
description: factorise an expression fully by taking out the highest common factor, including letters, such as 12x − 18 = 6(2x − 3) and 5x² + 15x = 5x(x + 3), and check by expanding.
instruction: Give the pupil 8x + 12, 15a − 10b, x² − 6x and 6x²y + 9xy to factorise fully (4(2x + 3), 5(3a − 2b), x(x − 6) and 3xy(2x + 3)). If they take out only part of the common factor, as in 2(4x + 6), ask whether what is left in the bracket still has a common factor. Ask them to check every answer by expanding.

name: Expand products of binomials
description: expand and simplify the product of two binomials, such as (x + 3)(x − 5) and (2x − 1)², and of three, such as (x + 1)(x + 2)(x + 3).
instruction: Give the pupil (x + 4)(x + 2), (x + 3)(x − 5), (2x − 1)² and (x − 6)(x + 6) to expand, using a grid if it helps (x² + 6x + 8, x² − 2x − 15, 4x² − 4x + 1 and x² − 36). Ask why (x + 3)² is not x² + 9, using the area of a square with side x + 3. If that goes well, try (x + 1)(x + 2)(x + 3) = x³ + 6x² + 11x + 6.

name: Write expressions and formulae from a situation
description: turn a situation or a procedure described in words into an algebraic expression or formula, such as the cost of n tickets at £8 each plus a £3 booking fee, C = 8n + 3.
instruction: Describe some situations and ask the pupil to write an expression or formula for each: the perimeter of a rectangle that is 3 cm longer than it is wide (P = 4w + 6 if the width is w), the cost of hiring a bike for £12 plus £4.50 an hour, and the trick 'think of a number, double it and add 5'. Then reverse it: give 2(n + 4) and ask them to describe a situation or a number trick it could stand for.

name: Solving an equation
description:
Solution of an equation: a value of the letter that makes both sides equal; x = 4 is the solution of 3x − 5 = 7.
Inverse operation: the operation that undoes another; addition and subtraction undo each other, and so do multiplication and division.
Balancing: doing the same operation to both sides of an equation keeps it true, which is how an equation is solved one step at a time.

name: Solve linear equations
description: solve linear equations in one unknown, including equations with the unknown on both sides, with brackets and with fractions, and check the solution by substituting it.
instruction: Give the pupil a set that gets harder, such as 5x + 3 = 28, 7 − 2x = 15, 4(x − 3) = 2x + 5 and (x + 2)/3 = x − 4, and ask them to write one step per line, saying what they did to both sides (x = 5, −4, 8.5 and 7). Ask them to check each solution by substitution, and point out that solutions can be negative or not whole numbers.

name: Form and solve equations from problems
description: form a linear equation from a problem about angles, lengths, ages or money, solve it, and interpret the answer in the context.
instruction: Give the pupil a problem such as: the angles of a triangle are x, 2x and x + 40 degrees; find each angle (35°, 70° and 75°). Then a money problem: Sam has £14 more than Priya, and together they have £50; how much does each have (Priya £18, Sam £32)? Ask them to say what the letter stands for, write the equation, solve it and check that the answer makes sense.

name: Change the subject of a formula
description: rearrange a formula to make a different letter the subject, such as making a the subject of v = u + at or r the subject of A = πr².
instruction: Give the pupil formulae to rearrange, such as P = 2l + 2w for w, v = u + at for a, and F = 9C/5 + 32 for C, and ask them to treat each like an equation, doing the same to both sides. Then ask them to check one rearranged formula with numbers. If that goes well, try A = πr² for r (r = √(A/π)).

name: Sequence and its rules
description:
Sequence: an ordered list of numbers, called terms, that follows a rule.
Term-to-term rule: a rule that gives each term from the one before, such as 'add 4'.
Position-to-term rule (nth term): a rule that gives any term from its position n, such as 4n − 1, which makes the 10th term 39.

name: Arithmetic, geometric and special sequences
description:
Arithmetic sequence: a sequence in which the same number is added each time, such as 5, 8, 11, 14, …; the number added is the common difference.
Geometric sequence: a sequence in which each term is multiplied by the same number to give the next, such as 3, 6, 12, 24, …
Special sequences: the square numbers 1, 4, 9, 16, …, the cube numbers 1, 8, 27, …, the triangular numbers 1, 3, 6, 10, …, and Fibonacci-type sequences, where each term is the sum of the two before it.

name: Generate and continue sequences
description: generate the terms of a sequence from a term-to-term rule or a position-to-term rule, and continue arithmetic, geometric and other common sequences, describing the rule in words.
instruction: Give the pupil a term-to-term rule ('start at 7 and subtract 3') and a position-to-term rule (n² + 1), and ask for the first five terms of each (7, 4, 1, −2, −5 and 2, 5, 10, 17, 26). Then give 2, 6, 18, 54, …, 1, 3, 6, 10, … and 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, … to continue and name, and ask them to describe each rule in words.

name: Find the nth term of an arithmetic sequence
description: find the nth term of an arithmetic sequence, and use it to find any term or to decide whether a given number is in the sequence.
instruction: Give the pupil 5, 8, 11, 14, … and ask for the nth term (3n + 2), the 50th term (152) and whether 100 is in the sequence (no, because 3n = 98 has no whole-number solution). Ask them to explain where each number in 3n + 2 comes from, for example using the 'zeroth term'. Then try a decreasing sequence such as 20, 16, 12, 8, … (24 − 4n).

name: Coordinates in four quadrants
description:
Coordinate grid: two number lines at right angles, the x-axis across and the y-axis up, crossing at the origin (0, 0) and dividing the plane into four quadrants.
Coordinates: a pair (x, y) that gives a point's position; the first number is the distance across and the second the distance up or down, so (−3, 2) is 3 to the left of the origin and 2 up.

name: Straight-line graph, gradient and intercept
description:
Linear function: a relationship whose graph is a straight line, with an equation of the form y = mx + c.
Gradient: the steepness of the line, m, which is the change in y when x increases by 1; it is positive if the line goes up from left to right and negative if it goes down.
y-intercept: the point where the line crosses the y-axis, (0, c).

name: Draw a straight-line graph
description: draw the graph of a linear function such as y = 2x − 3 from a table of values, with suitable scales on the axes, and recognise lines such as x = 4, y = −1 and y = −x.
instruction: Ask the pupil to make a table of values for y = 2x − 3 for x from −2 to 3 (y from −7 to 3), plot the points and join them with a ruler, and describe the graph. Ask what it would mean if one point did not lie on the line. Then ask what the lines x = 4, y = −1 and y = −x look like, and where y = 2x − 3 crosses y = −1 (at (1, −1)).

name: Find the gradient and intercept of a line
description: find the gradient and y-intercept of a straight line from its graph, from two points on it or from its equation, rearranging an equation such as 2y − 4x = 6 into the form y = mx + c first, and say what the gradient means in a context.
instruction: Tell the pupil that a line passes through (0, −1) and (2, 5), and ask for its gradient, y-intercept and equation (y = 3x − 1). Then give 2y − 4x = 6 and 3x + y = 7 to rearrange and read off m and c (y = 2x + 3 and y = −3x + 7). Finish with a context, such as a taxi fare C = 2.5d + 3 in pounds for d miles, and ask what 2.5 and 3 mean.

name: Quadratic function and parabola
description:
Quadratic function: a relationship whose equation has x² as its highest power, such as y = x² − 2x − 3.
Parabola: the U-shaped graph of a quadratic function (∩-shaped when the x² term is negative); it is symmetrical about a vertical line through its turning point, the lowest or highest point of the curve.

name: Draw the graph of a quadratic function
description: draw the graph of a quadratic function from a table of values, including negative values of x, join the points with a smooth curve, and read off the line of symmetry, the turning point and where the curve crosses the axes.
instruction: Ask the pupil to make a table for y = x² − 2x − 3 for x from −2 to 4 (y = 5, 0, −3, −4, −3, 0, 5), plot the points and join them with a smooth curve rather than straight lines. Ask for the turning point (1, −4), the line of symmetry x = 1, and where the graph crosses the axes. Pay attention to x = −2: (−2)² = 4, so y = 4 + 4 − 3 = 5.

name: Use graphs to estimate solutions
description: use linear and quadratic graphs to find y for a given x and x for a given y, to find approximate solutions to equations, and to estimate the solution of a pair of simultaneous linear equations from the point where the lines cross.
instruction: Using the graph of y = x² − 2x − 3, ask the pupil to estimate the values of x where y = 2 and explain why there are two (about −1.4 and 3.4). Then ask them to draw y = x + 1 and y = 7 − x on the same axes, read off where they cross (3, 4), and check that the point fits both equations. Make clear that a value read from a graph is an estimate.

name: Interpret graphs of real situations
description: interpret graphs of real situations, including piecewise linear graphs such as distance–time graphs, exponential growth curves and reciprocal curves, read approximate answers from them, and explain what the gradient shows.
instruction: Describe a walk: 2 km in the first 30 minutes, a 15-minute rest, then 3 km more in 45 minutes. Ask the pupil to sketch the distance–time graph, say what each section means, and work out the speed on each moving part (4 km/h both times). Then describe a graph of bacteria doubling every hour and a graph of journey time against speed for a 120 km trip (t = 120/v), and ask them to describe the shape of each and read off some approximate values.

name: Metric units and time
description:
1 km: 1,000 m
1 m: 100 cm
1 cm: 10 mm
1 kg: 1,000 g
1 tonne: 1,000 kg
1 litre: 1,000 ml
1 cm³: 1 ml
1 litre: 1,000 cm³
1 m²: 10,000 cm²
1 cm²: 100 mm²
1 m³: 1,000,000 cm³
1 hour: 60 minutes
1 minute: 60 seconds
1 day: 24 hours

name: Convert between units
description: convert between metric units of length, mass, capacity, area and volume, and between units of time, including decimal quantities, such as 2.4 kg = 2,400 g, 3.5 m² = 35,000 cm² and 1.25 hours = 1 hour 15 minutes.
instruction: Give the pupil conversions to do, such as 2.4 kg to g, 650 mm to m, 0.75 litres to ml, 3.5 m² to cm² and 2.3 hours to hours and minutes (2,400 g, 0.65 m, 750 ml, 35,000 cm² and 2 hours 18 minutes). For the area conversion, ask them to picture a 1 m by 1 m square to see why the factor is 10,000 and not 100. Watch for 2.3 hours being read as 2 hours 30 minutes.

name: Express one quantity as a fraction or percentage of another
description: express one quantity as a fraction or a percentage of another, converting to the same units first, including results greater than 1 or more than 100%, and compare two quantities using percentages.
instruction: Ask the pupil what fraction 45 minutes is of 2 hours (3/8), and what percentage 36 is of 48 (75%). Then ask them to compare two test scores, 17 out of 25 and 26 out of 40, using percentages (68% and 65%), and finally to express 75 g as a percentage of 60 g (125%).

name: Ratio
description:
Ratio: a comparison of the sizes of two or more quantities, written a : b; a ratio of 2 : 3 means 2 parts of the first for every 3 parts of the second.
Simplest form: a ratio written with whole numbers that have no common factor, such as 4 : 6 = 2 : 3.
Part to part and part to whole: in a ratio of 2 : 3, the first quantity is 2/3 of the second and 2/5 of the whole.

name: Simplify a ratio
description: simplify a ratio, including ratios with different units, decimals or fractions, and write a ratio in the form 1 : n.
instruction: Give the pupil ratios to simplify, such as 18 : 24, 45 cm : 2 m, 0.6 : 1.5 and ½ : ¾ (3 : 4, 9 : 40, 2 : 5 and 2 : 3). Ask them to explain why the units have to be the same first. Then ask for 4 : 10 in the form 1 : n (1 : 2.5).

name: Divide a quantity in a ratio
description: divide a quantity in a given ratio, and find the other parts or the whole when one part is known.
instruction: Ask the pupil to share £180 in the ratio 4 : 5 (£80 and £100), and 2.4 kg of flour in the ratio 1 : 2 : 3 (0.4 kg, 0.8 kg and 1.2 kg). Then turn it round: sand and cement are mixed in the ratio 5 : 2, and 15 kg of sand is used; how much cement is needed, and how much mixture is made (6 kg and 21 kg)? Suggest a bar model if they get stuck.

name: Direct and inverse proportion
description:
Direct proportion: two quantities are in direct proportion if one is always the same multiple of the other, y = kx, so doubling one doubles the other; the graph is a straight line through the origin.
Inverse proportion: two quantities are in inverse proportion if their product is always the same, xy = k, so doubling one halves the other; the graph is a curve that never meets the axes.

name: Solve proportion problems
description: solve problems with direct and inverse proportion, such as recipes, best buys and workers sharing a job, using the unitary method or a multiplier, recognise proportion in a table or a graph, and write the relationship as a formula.
instruction: Give the pupil a recipe problem (a cake for 6 people needs 240 g of flour; how much for 15? 600 g), a best-buy problem (500 g for £2.35 or 750 g for £3.45; the larger pack is cheaper per gram) and an inverse problem (4 painters take 9 days; how long would 6 painters take? 6 days). For each, ask whether doubling one quantity doubles or halves the other. Then give a table of x and y values and ask whether it shows direct proportion, inverse proportion or neither, and for the formula.

name: Percentage change and multiplier
description:
Percentage change: an increase or decrease written as a percentage of the original amount.
Multiplier: the number you multiply the original amount by to apply a percentage change; an increase of 12% gives the multiplier 1.12, and a decrease of 12% gives 0.88.

name: Work with percentage increase and decrease
description: increase or decrease an amount by a percentage, by finding the change or by using a multiplier, and work out a change as a percentage of the original amount.
instruction: Ask the pupil to increase £240 by 15% and decrease 85 kg by 20%, once by finding the change and once with a multiplier (£276 and 68 kg). Then ask for the percentage change when a bike is reduced from £320 to £272 (a 15% decrease) and a plant grows from 8 cm to 20 cm (a 150% increase); watch for dividing by the new amount. Finish with: a price rises by 10% and then falls by 10%; is it back where it started? Let them test it on £100.

name: Find the original amount after a percentage change
description: find the original amount when the amount after a percentage increase or decrease is known.
instruction: Give the pupil a problem such as: in a 20% sale a coat costs £64; what was the original price? Ask them first to explain why adding 20% of £64 gives the wrong answer, then to solve it with the multiplier 0.8 (£80). Follow with an increase: a salary is £27,300 after a 5% rise; what was it before (£26,000)?

name: Calculate simple interest
description: calculate simple interest, where the same amount of interest is added each year as a percentage of the amount first invested, and find the total after a number of years or the time needed to earn a given amount.
instruction: Explain simple interest briefly: the interest is the same amount every year, a percentage of the amount first put in. Ask the pupil for the simple interest on £1,500 at 3% a year for 4 years, and the total (£180 and £1,680). Then ask how long it would take £2,000 at 2.5% simple interest to earn £300 (6 years).

name: Compound units: speed, density and unit price
description:
Speed: distance travelled per unit of time, speed = distance ÷ time, in units such as km/h or m/s.
Density: mass per unit of volume, density = mass ÷ volume, in units such as g/cm³.
Unit price: the cost of one unit of a product, such as £ per kg or pence per 100 g.

name: Solve problems with compound units
description: solve problems with speed, density and unit pricing, rearranging the formula when needed and converting units, such as km/h to m/s.
instruction: Ask the pupil: a car travels 135 km in 1 hour 30 minutes; what is its average speed (90 km/h)? Then: a block of metal has a volume of 40 cm³ and a mass of 316 g; what is its density, and what would 100 cm³ of the metal weigh (7.9 g/cm³ and 790 g)? Finally ask them to convert 72 km/h to m/s (20 m/s) and explain each step.

name: Use scale drawings and maps
description: use scale factors, scale drawings and maps to find real lengths and distances, and make a simple scale drawing.
instruction: Give the pupil a map with scale 1 : 25,000 and ask how far 6.4 cm on the map is in real life, in kilometres (1.6 km), and how long a 3 km path would be on the map (12 cm). Then ask how they would make a scale drawing of a 6 m by 4.5 m classroom using 1 cm to 50 cm (12 cm by 9 cm).

name: Lines, angles and labelling
description:
Line segment: the part of a line between two end points, named by those points, such as AB.
Parallel lines: lines that stay the same distance apart and never meet, marked with matching arrows.
Perpendicular lines: lines that meet at a right angle (90°).
Acute, obtuse and reflex angles: an acute angle is less than 90°, an obtuse angle is between 90° and 180°, and a reflex angle is between 180° and 360°.
Labelling a triangle: the vertices are named with capital letters, as in triangle ABC; the angle at B is written ∠ABC, and the side opposite A is often called a.

name: Measure and draw lines, angles and triangles
description: measure and draw line segments and angles accurately, including reflex angles, and construct a triangle from three sides, from two sides and the angle between them, or from two angles and the side between them.
instruction: Ask the pupil to describe how they would measure an angle of about 140° and a reflex angle of 250° with a 180° protractor, and which scale they would read. Then ask them to explain step by step how to construct triangle ABC with AB = 7 cm, BC = 5 cm and AC = 6 cm using a ruler and compasses, and how to draw a triangle from two sides and the angle between them. If they have paper and equipment, let them do it and report what they measure.

name: Triangles and quadrilaterals
description:
Isosceles triangle: a triangle with two equal sides and two equal angles.
Equilateral triangle: a triangle with three equal sides and three angles of 60°.
Parallelogram: a quadrilateral with two pairs of parallel sides; its opposite sides and opposite angles are equal.
Rhombus: a parallelogram with four equal sides; its diagonals cross at right angles.
Rectangle and square: a rectangle is a parallelogram with four right angles, and a square is a rectangle with four equal sides.
Kite: a quadrilateral with two pairs of equal sides next to each other.
Trapezium: a quadrilateral with one pair of parallel sides.

name: Polygons and symmetry
description:
Polygon: a closed 2-D shape with straight sides, named by its number of sides: pentagon (5), hexagon (6), octagon (8), decagon (10).
Regular polygon: a polygon with all its sides equal and all its angles equal.
Interior and exterior angle: the interior angle is the angle inside the polygon at a vertex; the exterior angle is between one side and the next side extended, and the two add up to 180°.
Line symmetry: a shape has a line of symmetry if one half is the mirror image of the other.
Rotational symmetry: a shape has rotational symmetry of order n if it looks the same n times during a full turn about its centre.

name: Angles and parallel lines
description:
Vertically opposite angles: the pairs of opposite angles where two straight lines cross; they are equal.
Alternate angles: angles on opposite sides of a line crossing two parallel lines, both between the parallel lines (a Z shape); they are equal.
Corresponding angles: angles in matching positions where a line crosses two parallel lines (an F shape); they are equal.
Co-interior angles: angles on the same side of the crossing line, both between the parallel lines (a C shape); they add up to 180°.

name: Angle facts
description:
angles on a straight line: add up to 180°
angles around a point: add up to 360°
vertically opposite angles: are equal
angles in a triangle: add up to 180°
angles in a quadrilateral: add up to 360°
alternate angles on parallel lines: are equal
corresponding angles on parallel lines: are equal
co-interior angles on parallel lines: add up to 180°
base angles of an isosceles triangle: are equal
exterior angles of any polygon: add up to 360°

name: Find missing angles and give reasons
description: find missing angles in diagrams with straight lines, parallel lines, triangles and quadrilaterals, and give a reason for each step using the correct angle fact.
instruction: Describe a diagram in words: two parallel lines crossed by a third line, with one of the eight angles marked 65°, and ask the pupil to find the other seven, naming the fact behind each (they are all 65° or 115°). Then give an isosceles triangle with an angle of 40° between the two equal sides, and ask for the other two angles (70° each). Insist on a reason for every step, such as 'alternate angles are equal', not just the number.

name: Find angles in polygons
description: work out the sum of the interior angles of any polygon by splitting it into triangles, (n − 2) × 180°, and find the interior and exterior angles of regular polygons.
instruction: Ask the pupil to split a pentagon into triangles from one vertex and explain why its angles add up to 540°. Then ask for the interior and exterior angles of a regular hexagon (120° and 60°) and a regular decagon (144° and 36°). Finish with the reverse: a regular polygon has exterior angles of 24°; how many sides does it have (15)?

name: Congruent triangles
description:
Congruent shapes: shapes that are exactly the same shape and size, so that one fits exactly on top of the other, if necessary after turning it over.
Conditions for congruent triangles: two triangles are congruent if they match in three sides (SSS), two sides and the angle between them (SAS), two angles and a corresponding side (ASA or AAS), or a right angle, the hypotenuse and one other side (RHS).

name: Construct bisectors and perpendiculars
description: construct with ruler and compasses the perpendicular bisector of a line segment, the bisector of an angle, and the perpendicular to a line from or at a given point, explain why each construction works, and use the fact that the shortest distance from a point to a line is along the perpendicular.
instruction: Ask the pupil to describe step by step how to construct the perpendicular bisector of an 8 cm line segment and the bisector of an angle of 70°, and to say which arcs must have the same radius. Then ask them to explain why the construction works, using congruent triangles or the properties of a rhombus. If they have equipment, let them do it and check with a protractor that the angles come out as 90° and 35°.

name: Prove simple geometric results
description: use angle facts, properties of shapes and congruence to prove simple results, such as that the angles in a triangle add up to 180° or that the opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal, giving a reason for each step.
instruction: Start with the angle sum of a triangle: ask the pupil to imagine a line through one vertex parallel to the opposite side and explain, using alternate angles, why the three angles of the triangle together make a straight line. Then ask them to prove that the opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal, and that an exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the two interior angles opposite it. Make clear that measuring a few drawings is not a proof, and ask for a reason at every step.

name: Transformations
description:
Reflection: a transformation that flips a shape over a mirror line.
Rotation: a transformation that turns a shape through an angle, clockwise or anticlockwise, about a fixed point, the centre of rotation.
Translation: a transformation that slides a shape without turning it, described by how far it moves left or right and up or down.
Enlargement: a transformation that changes the size of a shape by a scale factor from a centre of enlargement; lengths are multiplied by the scale factor and angles stay the same.

name: Reflect, rotate and translate shapes
description: reflect, rotate and translate a shape on a coordinate grid, describe fully the single transformation that maps one shape onto another, and say which properties stay the same.
instruction: Give the pupil a triangle with vertices (1, 1), (4, 1) and (1, 3), and ask for the new vertices after a reflection in the y-axis ((−1, 1), (−4, 1), (−1, 3)), a rotation of 90° clockwise about the origin ((1, −1), (1, −4), (3, −1)) and a translation 3 left and 2 up ((−2, 3), (1, 3), (−2, 5)). Then describe a shape and its image and ask them to name the transformation fully, with the mirror line, the angle, direction and centre, or the movement. Ask what stays the same between a shape and its image in every case.

name: Similar shapes
description: Similar shapes: shapes where one is an enlargement of the other; corresponding angles are equal, and all corresponding lengths are in the same ratio, given by the scale factor.

name: Enlarge a shape and use similarity
description: enlarge a shape by a positive scale factor, including a fraction, from a centre of enlargement, with and without a coordinate grid, and use the scale factor to find missing lengths in similar shapes.
instruction: Give the pupil a triangle with vertices (1, 1), (3, 1) and (1, 2), and ask for the vertices after an enlargement with scale factor 3 from the origin ((3, 3), (9, 3), (3, 6)), and with scale factor ½ from (1, 1) ((1, 1), (2, 1), (1, 1.5)). Then give two similar rectangles, 4 cm by 6 cm and 10 cm by x cm, and ask for the scale factor and x (2.5 and 15). Ask whether the area is multiplied by the same scale factor, and why not.

name: Parts of a circle and π
description:
Radius and diameter: the radius is the distance from the centre of a circle to its edge; the diameter is a line across the circle through the centre, twice as long as the radius.
Circumference: the perimeter of a circle.
π (pi): the circumference of any circle divided by its diameter, about 3.14159; its decimals never end and never repeat.

name: Area and volume formulae
description:
area of a rectangle: length × width
area of a parallelogram: base × perpendicular height
area of a triangle: ½ × base × perpendicular height
area of a trapezium: ½(a + b)h, where a and b are the parallel sides and h is the distance between them
circumference of a circle: πd, or 2πr
area of a circle: πr²
volume of a cuboid: length × width × height
volume of a prism: area of cross-section × length
volume of a cylinder: πr²h

name: Calculate perimeters and areas of polygons
description: calculate the perimeter and area of triangles, parallelograms, trapezia and shapes made from them, explain where the area formulae come from, and work backwards from an area to a missing length.
instruction: Give the pupil a triangle with base 9 cm and perpendicular height 6 cm, a parallelogram with base 7.5 cm and height 4 cm, and a trapezium with parallel sides of 5 cm and 11 cm that are 6 cm apart (27 cm², 30 cm² and 48 cm²). Ask them to explain why the triangle formula has a half in it, by putting two identical triangles together to make a parallelogram. Then give an L-shaped room to split into rectangles, and a triangle with an area of 24 cm² and a base of 8 cm, asking for its height (6 cm).

name: Calculate the circumference and area of a circle
description: calculate the circumference and area of a circle, and the perimeter and area of semicircles and shapes with circular parts, giving answers in terms of π or rounded sensibly.
instruction: Ask the pupil for the circumference and area of a circle with radius 5 cm, first in terms of π and then to 1 decimal place (10π ≈ 31.4 cm and 25π ≈ 78.5 cm²). Then give a circle with diameter 12 cm and ask for its area (36π ≈ 113.1 cm²), watching for the radius and diameter being mixed up. Finish with a running track: a rectangle 100 m by 60 m with a semicircle on each short side; how far is it round the outside (200 + 60π ≈ 388.5 m)?

name: 3-D shapes
description:
Face, edge and vertex: a face is a flat or curved surface of a 3-D shape, an edge is where two faces meet, and a vertex is a corner (plural vertices).
Prism: a 3-D shape with the same cross-section all along its length, such as a cuboid or a triangular prism; a cylinder is like a prism with a circular cross-section.
Pyramid, cone and sphere: a pyramid has a polygon base and triangular faces meeting at a point, a cone has a circular base and a curved surface meeting at a point, and a sphere is a perfectly round ball.
Net: a 2-D pattern that folds up to make a 3-D shape.

name: Calculate volume and surface area
description: calculate the volume of cuboids, other prisms and cylinders as area of cross-section × length, find the surface area of cuboids and other prisms using a net, and convert between cm³ and litres.
instruction: Ask the pupil how many faces, edges and vertices a triangular prism has (5, 9 and 6). Then ask for the volume and surface area of a cuboid 8 cm by 5 cm by 3 cm (120 cm³ and 158 cm²), explaining the surface area with a net. Then give a triangular prism whose cross-section is a right-angled triangle with shorter sides 6 cm and 8 cm and whose length is 20 cm (480 cm³), and a cylinder with radius 4 cm and height 10 cm (160π ≈ 502.7 cm³), and ask how many litres the cylinder holds (about 0.5 litres).

name: Pythagoras' theorem
description:
Hypotenuse: the longest side of a right-angled triangle, opposite the right angle.
Pythagoras' theorem: in a right-angled triangle, the square of the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides, a² + b² = c², where c is the hypotenuse.

name: Explain a proof of Pythagoras' theorem
description: explain a proof of Pythagoras' theorem, such as one that arranges four copies of a right-angled triangle inside a square, and explain why checking a few triangles is not enough.
instruction: Ask the pupil to picture four copies of a right-angled triangle with shorter sides a and b and hypotenuse c, placed inside a square of side a + b so that they leave a tilted square of side c in the middle. Ask them to write the area of the big square in two ways, (a + b)² and 4 × ½ab + c², and to simplify until a² + b² = c² appears. Then ask why measuring a few triangles would not prove the theorem.

name: Use Pythagoras' theorem
description: use Pythagoras' theorem to find a missing side of a right-angled triangle, the hypotenuse or a shorter side, in diagrams and in context, and decide whether a triangle with given sides is right-angled.
instruction: Give the pupil a right-angled triangle with shorter sides 9 cm and 12 cm and ask for the hypotenuse (15 cm), then one with hypotenuse 13 cm and one side 5 cm and ask for the third side (12 cm). Ask how they decide whether to add or subtract the squares. Then a problem: a 5 m ladder leans against a wall with its foot 1.4 m from the wall; how high up the wall does it reach (4.8 m)? Finish by asking whether a triangle with sides 7 cm, 9 cm and 11 cm is right-angled (no: 49 + 81 = 130, not 121).

name: Sine, cosine and tangent
description:
Opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse: for a chosen angle θ in a right-angled triangle, the opposite side is across from θ, the adjacent side is next to θ but is not the hypotenuse, and the hypotenuse is the longest side.
Sine, cosine and tangent: sin θ = opposite ÷ hypotenuse, cos θ = adjacent ÷ hypotenuse and tan θ = opposite ÷ adjacent, often remembered as SOH CAH TOA; because all right-angled triangles with the same angle θ are similar, these ratios depend only on θ.

name: Use trigonometry in right-angled triangles
description: use sine, cosine and tangent to find a missing side or angle in a right-angled triangle, with the calculator set to degrees, and solve problems such as heights and slopes.
instruction: Give the pupil a right-angled triangle with hypotenuse 10 cm and an angle of 35°, and ask for the side opposite the angle (10 sin 35° ≈ 5.74 cm). Then one with opposite side 7 cm and adjacent side 4 cm, and ask for the angle (about 60.3°). Ask them to label the sides first and say which ratio they chose and why. Then a problem: from 30 m away, the top of a tree is seen at an angle of elevation of 28°; how far is the top of the tree above eye level (about 16.0 m)? Remind them to check that the calculator is in degree mode.

name: Probability
description:
Probability: a number from 0 to 1 that measures how likely an outcome is; 0 means impossible, 1 means certain and ½ means an even chance, and it can be written as a fraction, a decimal or a percentage.
Equally likely outcomes: outcomes that each have the same chance, such as the six faces of a fair dice; a dice or spinner where they do not is biased.
Sum of probabilities: the probabilities of all the possible outcomes, when exactly one of them must happen, add up to 1, so P(not A) = 1 − P(A).

name: Estimate probabilities from an experiment
description: record the results of a probability experiment in a frequency table, work out the relative frequency of each outcome (the number of times it happened divided by the number of trials), compare it with the theoretical probability, and decide whether a dice or spinner seems fair.
instruction: Tell the pupil that a spinner with four equal sections was spun 200 times and landed on red 71 times, blue 45, green 42 and yellow 42. Ask for the relative frequency of each colour (0.355, 0.225, 0.21 and 0.21), what they would expect from a fair spinner (50 each), whether this spinner seems fair, and what they would do to be more confident. Ask why the estimate usually improves with more spins.

name: List outcomes systematically
description: list all the outcomes of one or two events systematically, in a list, a two-way table or a sample space grid.
instruction: Ask the pupil to list every outcome when a coin is tossed and a dice is rolled (12 outcomes), and to explain how they made sure they had them all. Then ask them to describe a sample space grid for the total of two dice and say how many outcomes it has (36).

name: Calculate theoretical probabilities
description: calculate theoretical probabilities of single and combined events from equally likely outcomes, as the number of favourable outcomes divided by the total number of outcomes, and use P(not A) = 1 − P(A).
instruction: Using the sample space grid for the total of two dice, ask the pupil for P(total of 7), P(total of 10 or more) and P(not a double) (1/6, 1/6 and 5/6). Ask which total is most likely and why. Then ask why P(total of 2) is not 1/11, even though there are eleven possible totals (it is 1/36).

name: Sets and Venn diagrams
description:
Set: a collection of things, called elements, such as the set of even numbers less than 10, {2, 4, 6, 8}.
Venn diagram: a diagram that shows sets as overlapping circles inside a rectangle that stands for everything being considered, the universal set ξ.
Intersection and union: the intersection A ∩ B is everything in both A and B; the union A ∪ B is everything in A or B or both.

name: Use Venn diagrams and two-way tables
description: sort items into a Venn diagram or a two-way table, count the elements in intersections and unions, and find probabilities from them.
instruction: Ask the pupil to sort the whole numbers from 1 to 20 into a Venn diagram with A = multiples of 3 and B = even numbers, and say what is in A ∩ B ({6, 12, 18}) and how many numbers are in A ∪ B (13). Then ask for the probability that a number picked at random from 1 to 20 is in A ∩ B (3/20). Finish with a frequency version: in a class of 30, 18 play football, 12 play netball and 5 play both; how many play neither (5)?

name: Types of data
description:
Categorical data: data in categories described in words, such as favourite sport.
Discrete data: numerical data that can only take particular values, usually counts, such as the number of siblings.
Continuous data: numerical data that is measured and can take any value in a range, such as height or time.
Grouped data: numerical data sorted into classes, such as 150 ≤ h < 160, when there are too many different values to list one by one.

name: Averages, range and outliers
description:
Mean: the total of the values divided by the number of values.
Median: the middle value when the values are in order; with an even number of values, it is halfway between the middle two.
Mode: the value that occurs most often.
Range: the largest value minus the smallest, a measure of how spread out the data are.
Outlier: a value much larger or smaller than the rest, which can distort the mean and the range.

name: Calculate averages and the range
description: find the mean, median, mode and range of a set of data and of data in a frequency table, and explain how an outlier affects each of them.
instruction: Give the pupil the data 12, 7, 15, 9, 12, 21, 8, 12 and ask for the mean, median, mode and range (12, 12, 12 and 14). Then add an outlier, 75, and ask which measures change a lot and which hardly change (the mean becomes 19 and the range 68, while the median and mode stay at 12). Finally give a frequency table of goals scored in 20 matches (0 goals: 4 matches, 1: 7, 2: 5, 3: 3, 4: 1) and ask for the mean and the median (1.5 and 1).

name: Organise data in frequency tables
description: organise data in a frequency table using tallies, and group numerical data into classes of equal width written with inequalities, such as 20 ≤ t < 30.
instruction: Give the pupil 20 test marks out of 50: 34, 41, 27, 38, 45, 22, 31, 36, 48, 29, 33, 40, 25, 37, 44, 30, 39, 28, 35, 42. Ask them to make a grouped frequency table with the classes 20 ≤ m < 30, 30 ≤ m < 40 and 40 ≤ m < 50 (frequencies 5, 9 and 6). Ask where a mark of exactly 30 goes and why the classes must not overlap. Then ask for the modal class.

name: Draw and interpret bar charts and pictograms
description: draw and interpret bar charts, pictograms and vertical line charts for categorical and ungrouped numerical data, and bar charts for grouped data, with suitable scales and labels.
instruction: Describe a small data set, such as how 30 pupils travel to school, and ask the pupil how they would draw a bar chart and a pictogram for it, including the scale and the key. Then describe a bar chart in words and ask questions that need more than reading off one bar, such as the fraction of pupils who walk. Ask which kind of chart suits numerical data such as shoe sizes, and why the bars of a chart for categories should have gaps.

name: Draw and interpret pie charts
description: draw and interpret pie charts, working out the angle for each category as a fraction of 360°, and the frequency from an angle.
instruction: Give the pupil a frequency table, such as the favourite fruit of 40 people (apple 14, banana 10, orange 6, grapes 10), and ask them to work out the angle for each sector and check that they add up to 360° (126°, 90°, 54° and 90°). Then turn it round: in a pie chart for 72 people, the sector for 'bus' is 110°; how many people is that (22)? Ask why two pie charts for groups of different sizes cannot be compared just by the size of the sectors.

name: Compare two distributions
description: compare two sets of data using an average and the range, choose the most suitable average, and write the comparison in words that refer to the context.
instruction: Give the pupil the 100 m times of two classes: Class A has a mean of 15.2 s and a range of 4.1 s, and Class B a mean of 14.8 s and a range of 7.5 s. Ask them to write two sentences comparing them in context. Then give a data set with an outlier, such as house prices on one street, and ask which average represents it best and why. Push for sentences such as 'on average Class B was faster, but their times were more spread out'.

name: Scatter graphs and correlation
description:
Bivariate data: data with two values for each item, such as the height and arm span of each pupil.
Scatter graph: a graph with one point for each item, plotted from its two values.
Correlation: a pattern in which one variable tends to increase as the other increases (positive correlation) or decreases (negative correlation); no correlation means no such pattern, and correlation alone does not show that one causes the other.
Line of best fit: a straight line drawn through the middle of the points to show the trend.

name: Draw and use scatter graphs
description: plot a scatter graph, describe the correlation, draw a line of best fit by eye and use it to estimate values, and spot outliers.
instruction: Give the pupil eight pairs of data, such as hours of revision and test score, and ask how they would plot them, how they would describe the correlation, and where they would draw a line of best fit. Ask them to use the line to estimate the score for a given number of hours within the data, and discuss why an estimate far outside it, such as for 40 hours of revision, would not be reliable.

name: Judge what data can and cannot show
description: judge what can and cannot be concluded from data, charts and experiments, spotting misleading graphs, samples that are too small and correlation mistaken for cause, and explain the reasoning.
instruction: Give the pupil claims to judge, such as a bar chart in an advert whose vertical axis starts at 90%, 'ice cream sales and sunburn are correlated, so ice cream causes sunburn', and 'I rolled a dice six times and got no sixes, so it must be biased'. Ask them to explain what is wrong with each and what evidence would be needed for a sound conclusion.
